mcqs.question: Why can the same Spark application run unmodified on standalone, YARN, and Kubernetes cluster managers?
options: Because Spark rewrites its own source code to match each cluster manager at startup
Because all three cluster managers are actually the same software under different names
Because Spark's execution model never uses more than one executor regardless of cluster manager
Because Spark only cares that executors show up with requested resources — how the cluster manager finds and launches those executors is a separate concern the application doesn't need to know about
mcqs.explanation: The clean separation between "Spark needs resources" and "the cluster manager finds and provisions them" is exactly what lets the same application move across environments — Spark's driver and executors work identically once executors exist. The three cluster managers are genuinely different systems, Spark doesn't rewrite itself, and Spark applications routinely use many executors at once.

mcqs.question: What's a key practical difference between YARN and Spark's standalone cluster manager?
options: Standalone was specifically built to multiplex many different frameworks on shared hardware, while YARN only ever runs Spark
YARN was built as a general-purpose resource negotiator that multiplexes many frameworks (not just Spark) on shared hardware, while standalone is Spark's own simpler, typically Spark-only manager
Standalone requires Kubernetes to be installed as a prerequisite
YARN cannot allocate executors dynamically under any configuration
mcqs.explanation: YARN's defining strength is general-purpose multi-framework sharing on Hadoop-ecosystem clusters, while standalone is Spark's simpler built-in option typically used for dedicated, smaller Spark-only deployments — the roles described are reversed in the first option. Standalone doesn't require Kubernetes as a prerequisite, and YARN does support dynamic allocation.

mcqs.question: A job has a heavy shuffle stage followed by a light final aggregation. Why might dynamic allocation suit it better than static allocation?
options: Dynamic allocation lets the job hold the same fixed executor count throughout, guaranteeing predictability
Static allocation is not supported on any cluster manager for jobs with variable workloads
Dynamic allocation can request more executors during the heavy shuffle stage and release them during the lighter final stage, avoiding holding unused capacity for the job's less demanding portions
Dynamic allocation always runs faster than static allocation regardless of workload shape
mcqs.explanation: The scenario is exactly what dynamic allocation is designed for — resource needs varying meaningfully across a job's stages — letting it scale up when there's a real backlog and scale down when demand drops, rather than holding a fixed count throughout. Static allocation is supported everywhere and is sometimes the better, more predictable choice; it's holding a fixed count throughout that's the trait being described (that's static, not dynamic), and dynamic allocation isn't universally faster — its value is specifically for variable workloads.

mcqs.question: Two jobs on a shared cluster both use dynamic allocation and both experience a burst of work at the same time. What failure mode can result?
options: Both jobs automatically pause until the other finishes, guaranteeing no contention
The cluster manager always kills the smaller job to free resources for the larger one

Both jobs oscillate — scaling up, getting partially starved by the other's simultaneous scale-up, scaling back down — potentially performing worse than if both had used static allocation with a predictable fair share
Dynamic allocation is disabled automatically whenever two jobs run concurrently
mcqs.explanation: Competing dynamic-allocation jobs can genuinely oscillate against each other on a shared pool with no additional fairness layer, which is a real operational failure mode worse than the predictability static allocation would have given. Jobs don't automatically pause for each other, cluster managers don't reflexively kill the smaller job, and dynamic allocation isn't disabled just because multiple jobs run concurrently — it's the interaction between them that causes the problem.

mcqs.question: On Kubernetes, why would an executor handling a skewed, oversized partition get OOM-killed even though the cluster overall has spare memory available?
options: Kubernetes only allows one executor pod per node regardless of available memory
OOM-kills only happen when the entire cluster is out of memory, never for a single pod
The executor pod's memory limit was sized for a typical partition, and exceeding that pod-level limit gets it killed outright regardless of memory sitting unused elsewhere in the cluster
Executor pods automatically request more memory from the cluster whenever they approach their limit
mcqs.explanation: Kubernetes enforces a hard per-pod memory limit — exceeding it gets the pod killed regardless of how much memory is free elsewhere in the cluster, which is exactly the risk of sizing limits for a typical partition when the job has real skew. Multiple pods per node are completely normal, OOM-kills are a per-pod enforcement mechanism rather than requiring cluster-wide exhaustion, and pods don't get to unilaterally request more memory once running — the limit is a hard ceiling set in advance.
